title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle — Statement, Forms and Numericals
topicTitle: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle and concept of probability
notes: The three standard forms of the principle and the two numerical patterns NEB asks (electron in an atom; electron in the nucleus). The probability interpretation is in the main note.
• Position–momentum: $\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$, or with velocity $\Delta x\,\Delta v\ge\frac{h}{4\pi m}$.
• Energy–time: $\Delta E\,\Delta t\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$ — an excited state living Δt has a minimum energy spread ΔE, which broadens spectral lines (natural line width).
### Numerical pattern 1 — electron localised to atomic size

Δx = 10⁻¹⁰ m: Δv ≥ h/(4πmΔx) = 6.626×10⁻³⁴/(4π × 9.11×10⁻³¹ × 10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 5.8 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. This is comparable with the electron's own speed (2.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹), so a definite orbit is impossible — the standard argument against Bohr orbits.
### Numerical pattern 2 — electron inside the nucleus

Δx = 10⁻¹⁴ m (nuclear size): Δp ≈ h/(4πΔx) ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ kg m s⁻¹ → KE ≈ (Δp)²/2m ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ J ≈ 10⁹ eV. Nuclear binding energies are ~10⁷ eV, so the electron cannot be confined in the nucleus — proof that electrons are not nuclear constituents (β-particles are created at emission).

Because r and p cannot both be sharp, the electron's state is described by ψ with |ψ|² = probability density. The 1s radial probability peaks at 0.529 Å — Bohr's radius reappears as the *most probable* distance. 'Electron cloud', boundary surfaces and atomic radii averages all follow from this probabilistic description.
It matters only for microscopic particles: for a 1 g body at Δx = 10⁻¹⁰ m, Δv ≈ 10⁻²⁴ m s⁻¹ — utterly negligible, so classical mechanics remains valid for everyday objects.
confusion: ❌ The principle sets a limit on *both* quantities individually. ✅ Only the *product* of the two uncertainties is bounded; either one alone can be exact.
❌ ΔE·Δt means energy conservation is violated. ✅ It permits transient fluctuations within ΔE for times shorter than Δt — the basis of virtual processes and tunnelling.
❌ A better microscope can beat the limit. ✅ The limit is fundamental, not technical.

universalFacts: ħ = h/2π = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; the bound is often written Δx·Δp ≥ ħ/2 (numerically equal to h/4π).
Natural line width of an excited state (Δt ≈ 10⁻⁸ s): ΔE ≈ 10⁻⁸ eV — the origin of the intrinsic sharpness limit of spectral lines.
Tunnelling (STM, α-decay) is the practical use of the energy–time form.
examples: **Problem:** Δx = 5 × 10⁻¹¹ m for an electron — find Δv. **Solution:** Δv = h/(4πmΔx) = 6.626×10⁻³⁴/(4π × 9.11×10⁻³¹ × 5×10⁻¹¹) ≈ 1.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ — over half the orbital speed, confirming the orbit picture's collapse.
importantNotes: Write the form the question asks for (momentum or velocity); mixing m into the denominator wrongly is the common error.
Conclude numericals with the physical meaning (no definite orbit / no electron in the nucleus).

mcqs.question: The uncertainty principle is significant for:

summary: Heisenberg's principle has three standard forms: position–momentum Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π, or Δx·Δv ≥ h/4πm with velocity; energy–time ΔE·Δt ≥ h/4π; and angular momentum–angle ΔL·Δθ ≥ h/4π. Two numerical patterns carry the marks. First, an electron localised to atomic size, Δx = 10⁻¹⁰ m, has Δv ≥ h/(4πmΔx) ≈ 5.8 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹, comparable with its own 2.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹, so a definite orbit is impossible. Second, confining an electron to nuclear dimensions, Δx = 10⁻¹⁴ m, demands Δp ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ kg m s⁻¹ and a kinetic energy of order 10⁹ eV, far above nuclear binding energies of ~10⁷ eV, proving electrons are not nuclear constituents — β-particles are created during decay. The principle also forces the probability description, since r and p cannot both be sharp.
importantConcepts: Three forms: Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π, ΔE·Δt ≥ h/4π and ΔL·Δθ ≥ h/4π, with ħ = h/2π
Numerical pattern 1 — electron localised to 10⁻¹⁰ m gives Δv ≈ 5.8 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹, so no definite orbit
Numerical pattern 2 — electron confined to 10⁻¹⁴ m needs Δp ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ kg m s⁻¹ and KE ≈ 10⁹ eV
Probability concept: |ψ|² is the probability density, and 0.529 Å is the most probable 1s distance, not a fixed radius
Natural line width from ΔE·Δt with an excited-state lifetime Δt ≈ 10⁻⁸ s, and tunnelling as a practical consequence
importantStatements: Only the product of the uncertainties is bounded; either quantity alone may be exact.
The bound is fundamental, so a better microscope cannot reduce Δx·Δp below h/4π.
A fixed Bohr orbit would give Δx ≈ 0 together with Δp ≈ 0, which is impossible.
Nuclear binding energies are of order 10⁷ eV, far below the ≈10⁹ eV an electron confined in a nucleus would need.
For a 1 g body the uncertainty product is negligible, so classical mechanics remains valid for macroscopic objects.

keyPoints: Write both Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π and Δx·Δv ≥ h/4πm; questions often ask for the velocity form.
ΔE·Δt ≥ h/4π explains the natural width of spectral lines.
Conclude each numerical with its meaning: no definite orbit, or no electron in the nucleus.
The bound is often written Δx·Δp ≥ ħ/2, numerically identical to h/4π.
specialNotes: The energy–time form does not violate energy conservation; it allows transient fluctuations within ΔE for times shorter than Δt.
It is safest to state the principle as a property of quantum ensembles rather than committing to one interpretation.
A definite orbit fails because both conjugate quantities would be sharp, not because the orbit is curved.
examShortTricks: m belongs in the denominator only in the velocity form: Δv = h/(4πmΔx).
Use KE = (Δp)²/2m to convert a momentum uncertainty into the energy argument.
Write the physical conclusion as the last line of the numerical — that is where the marks are.
examNotes: The three forms plus one numerical application make a standard 4–5 mark question.
The two numerical patterns (atomic size, nuclear confinement) are the most examined 2–3 mark items.
One-mark questions usually ask whether the principle limits instruments — the answer is no.
